rv.q: “A Woman Among Women” is not just an exercise in transposition; it takes on a life of its own.
Centered by Dee Pelletier amid the true ensemble cast, A Woman Among Women swims through puzzling experimental choices before it lands with a bang.
It’s an ambitious mission, and this particular play has a compelling story to tell. It also has a striking “new form,” like Treplev’s play, that can get in the way of the storytelling.
A Woman Among Women, though, frustrates more than excites.
The bumper crop of plays about plays is becoming tiresome.

That said, to my old-school taste, the ambitious A Woman Among Women registers mostly as a terribly talky, at times even tedious, theater exercise that fails to engage pity or any emotion other than occasional confusion over who some of these people may be and what’s their relationship to the heroine, and why should I care?
And while I applaud the effort, the work falls well short of its ambitions.
Jonas has crafted a thoughtful, truthful meditation on parenthood, community, and the stories we tell to survive.
A Woman Among Women is an exceptional piece of writing, both in the context of All My Sons, and as a standalone piece.

A Woman Among Women is a mixed bag, with acerbic humor, disturbing situations, and a final reckoning that shakes the community to its core, infused with musical numbers that lengthen the show and break the mood and narrative flow with little reason.
While I wish that A Woman Among Women had embraced a single aesthetic approach and worn its inspiration more loosely, I admire how Jonas invites us to consider familiar conflicts in new ways.
Frustratingly slow to ignite, but genuinely thought-provoking once it does.

cn.t: Jonas's gender-flipped response to Miller's "All My Sons" divides critics: some praise its ambitious feminist reimagining and strong performances, while others find it a sluggish, overly reverent adaptation that lacks its own distinct voice.

vr.q: to invite that comparison to Arthur Miller just feels like you're setting yourself up for disappointment
While the crux of the piece does end up coming together and the exploration of morality and matriarchy is ripe with intrigue, it takes too long to get there.
